title: Ὄνος καὶ κόραξ καὶ λύκος
titleEn: The Donkey, the Raven and the Wolf
part: The Donkey, the Raven and the Wolf (Chambry 274 · Perry 190)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 274 (= Perry 190). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ὄνος ἡλκωμένος τὸν νῶτον ἔν τινι λειμῶνι ἐνέμετο.
sentences.tr: Onos hēlkōmenos ton nōton en tini leimōni enemeto.
sentences.l: A donkey, ulcerated as to his back, was grazing in a certain meadow.
sentences.i: A donkey with a raw sore on his back was grazing in a meadow.
sentences.n: τὸν νῶτον is an accusative of respect, naming the part affected — 'sore in respect of the back'. Greek uses it constantly for wounds, and English has no way to keep the case, so the literal line falls back on 'as to'. ἐνέμετο is the middle of νέμω: to have one's portion of pasture, hence to graze.

sentences.t: Κόρακος δὲ ἐπικαθίσαντος αὐτῷ καὶ τὸ ἕλκος κρούοντος, ὁ ὄνος ἀλγῶν ὠγκᾶτό τε καὶ ἐσκίρτα.
sentences.tr: Korakos de epikathisantos autōi kai to helkos krouontos, ho onos algōn ōnkato te kai eskirta.
sentences.l: And a raven having settled upon him and striking at the sore, the donkey, in pain, both brayed and leapt about.
sentences.i: And when a raven settled on him and set to pecking at the sore, the donkey in his pain brayed and leapt about.
sentences.n: The genitive absolute carries two participles of different tense: the aorist ἐπικαθίσαντος for the settling, done once, and the present κρούοντος for the pecking, which goes on. κρούω is to knock or strike, used here of the beak.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ ὀνηλάτου πόρρωθεν ἑστῶτος καὶ γελῶντος, λύκος παριὼν ἐθεάσατο καὶ πρὸς ἑαυτὸν ἔφη· « Ἄθλιοι ἡμεῖς, οἵ, κἂν αὐτὸ μόνον ὀφθῶμεν, διωκόμεθα, τούτους δὲ καὶ προσιόντας προσγελῶσιν. »
sentences.tr: Tou de onēlatou porrōthen hestōtos kai gelōntos, lykos pariōn etheasato kai pros heauton ephē· « Athlioi hēmeis, hoi, kan auto monon ophthōmen, diōkometha, toutous de kai prosiontas prosgelōsin. »
sentences.l: And the donkey-driver standing far off and laughing, a wolf passing by looked on and said to himself: « Wretched are we, who, if we are so much as merely seen, are hunted; but these they even smile upon as they come near. »
sentences.i: And with the driver standing at a distance and laughing, a wolf came past, watched, and said to himself: « What wretches we are — let us only be seen and we are hunted down; but these creatures they smile at even as they come up. »
sentences.n: κἂν is καὶ ἐάν run together, 'even if', and takes the subjunctive ὀφθῶμεν. αὐτὸ μόνον is adverbial, 'no more than that' — being seen is the whole of the wolf's offence. προσγελάω is to smile at someone in welcome, so the grievance is not that the raven escapes punishment but that it is made welcome. ἑστῶτος is the perfect participle of ἵστημι with present force: he has taken his stand and is standing there.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι οἱ κακοῦργοι τῶν ἀνθρώπων καὶ ἐξ αὐτῶν τῶν προσώπων καὶ ἐξ ἀπροόπτου δῆλοί εἰσιν.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti hoi kakourgoi tōn anthrōpōn kai ex autōn tōn prosōpōn kai ex aprooptou dēloi eisin.
sentences.l: The story shows that the evildoers among men are plain both from their very faces and unexpectedly.
sentences.i: The story shows that the evildoers among men are known from their very faces, and are found out at the moment no one is looking for it.
sentences.n: τῶν ἀνθρώπων is partitive, 'among men', which is how this corpus renders the closing formulas of this shape. ἐξ ἀπροόπτου is an adverbial phrase built on ἀπρόοπτος, 'unforeseen', and means simply 'unexpectedly' — there is no word for looking or glancing in it. The two καί set the face itself beside the unlooked-for moment: the wicked betray themselves by their look, and do so before anyone has thought to examine them. That is the wolf's own complaint turned into a rule — he is hunted the instant he is seen.
